choices.text: The partial structure that remains when a hydrogen atom is removed from an alkane
A stable compound made by removing a hydrogen from an alkane
choices.why: Alkyl groups are not stable compounds themselves; they are simply parts of larger compounds.

choices.text: An alkane with one extra hydrogen added
choices.why: An alkane already has the maximum number of hydrogens. An alkyl group has one hydrogen fewer.

choices.text: A functional group containing a carbon–carbon double bond
choices.why: Alkyl groups come from alkanes, which have only single bonds.

explanation: If you imagine removing a hydrogen atom from an alkane, the partial structure that remains is called an alkyl group. Alkyl groups are not stable compounds themselves; they are parts of larger compounds.

prompt: How is an alkyl group named from its parent alkane?

choices.text: The -ane ending of the alkane is replaced with -yl
The ending -yl is added after -ane, as in methaneyl
choices.why: The -ane ending is replaced, not kept: methane gives methyl.

choices.text: The ending -ene replaces -ane
choices.why: The alkyl group name ends in -yl, as in methyl and ethyl.

choices.text: The prefix alkyl- is put in front of the alkane name
choices.why: Alkyl groups are named by changing the ending: ethane becomes ethyl.

explanation: Alkyl groups are named by replacing the -ane ending of the parent alkane with an -yl ending. Removing a hydrogen from methane gives a methyl group, and from ethane an ethyl group.

choices.text: –CH2CH3
CH3CH3
choices.why: That is ethane, the parent alkane. The ethyl group has one hydrogen fewer and an open bond.

choices.text: –CH3
choices.why: That is the methyl group, from methane.

choices.text: –CH2CH2CH3
choices.why: That is the propyl group, from propane.

explanation: Removal of a hydrogen from ethane, CH3CH3, generates an ethyl group, –CH2CH3 (Table 3.3.1). Its abbreviation is Et.

prompt: According to Table 3.3.1, what is another name for the pentyl group, –CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3?

choices.text: Amyl
Butyl
choices.why: Butyl (Bu) is the four-carbon group, –CH2CH2CH2CH3.

choices.text: Propyl
choices.why: Propyl (Pr) is the three-carbon group, –CH2CH2CH3.

choices.text: Pentane
choices.why: Pentane is the parent alkane. The group's name ends in -yl.

explanation: Table 3.3.1 lists the straight-chain five-carbon group, –CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3, as pentyl, or amyl.

prompt: In Table 3.3.1, which alkyl group is abbreviated Bu?

choices.text: Butyl, –CH2CH2CH2CH3
Butane, CH3CH2CH2CH3
choices.why: The abbreviations stand for alkyl groups, not the parent alkanes.

choices.text: Propyl, –CH2CH2CH3
choices.why: Propyl is abbreviated Pr.

choices.text: Ethyl, –CH2CH3
choices.why: Ethyl is abbreviated Et.

explanation: Table 3.3.1 gives the abbreviations Me (methyl), Et (ethyl), Pr (propyl) and Bu (butyl, –CH2CH2CH2CH3).

prompt: How are branched alkyl groups, such as isopropyl, generated?

choices.text: By removing a hydrogen atom from an internal carbon
By removing a hydrogen atom from an end carbon
choices.why: Removing a hydrogen from an end carbon of a straight-chain alkane gives the straight-chain groups, such as propyl.

choices.text: By removing a carbon atom from the chain
choices.why: An alkyl group differs from its alkane by one hydrogen only; the carbons stay.

choices.text: By adding a hydrogen atom to an internal carbon
choices.why: Alkyl groups come from removing a hydrogen, never adding one.

explanation: Just as straight-chain alkyl groups are generated by removing a hydrogen from an end carbon, branched alkyl groups are generated by removing a hydrogen atom from an internal carbon.

prompt: How many different 3-carbon alkyl groups are possible?
explanation: Two 3-carbon alkyl groups are possible: propyl, from removing a hydrogen from an end carbon of propane, and isopropyl, from removing one from the internal carbon.

prompt: How many different 4-carbon alkyl groups are possible?
explanation: Four 4-carbon alkyl groups are possible (Figure 3.3.1): butyl and sec-butyl from butane, and isobutyl and tert-butyl from isobutane.

prompt: What makes a carbon atom tertiary (3°)?

choices.text: It is bonded to three other carbon atoms
It is bonded to three hydrogen atoms
choices.why: The classification counts attached carbons, not hydrogens. A carbon with three hydrogens (RCH3) is primary.

choices.text: It is the third carbon in the chain
choices.why: Position in the chain doesn't matter; what counts is how many other carbons are attached to it.

choices.text: It is part of a three-carbon molecule
choices.why: The term describes one carbon atom by the number of carbons bonded to it, not the size of the molecule.

explanation: Primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary carbons are bonded to one, two, three and four other carbons, respectively. A tertiary carbon is bonded to three other carbons.

prompt: In names like sec-butyl and tert-butyl, what do the prefixes sec- and tert- refer to?

choices.text: The number of other carbon atoms attached to the branching carbon atom
The number of hydrogens removed from the alkane
choices.why: Every alkyl group comes from removing just one hydrogen.

choices.text: The total number of carbons in the group
choices.why: sec-Butyl and tert-butyl both have four carbons; the prefixes describe how the branching carbon is attached.

choices.text: The second and third members of the alkane series
choices.why: sec- stands for secondary and tert- for tertiary, which classify a carbon by the carbons bonded to it.

explanation: The prefixes sec- (for secondary) and tert- (for tertiary) used for the C4 alkyl groups in Figure 3.3.1 refer to the number of other carbon atoms attached to the branching carbon atom.

prompt: What does the symbol R represent in organic structures?

choices.text: A generalized organic group, the rest of the molecule, which isn't specified
A radical, an atom with an unpaired electron
choices.why: In organic structures R stands for an unspecified organic group such as methyl, ethyl or propyl.

choices.text: Always a methyl group
choices.why: R can be methyl, ethyl, propyl, or any of a multitude of others.

choices.text: A hydrogen atom
choices.why: R is an organic group. In RCH3, for example, it marks a carbon attachment, which is why that carbon is primary.

explanation: The symbol R is used throughout organic chemistry to represent a generalized organic group. It can be methyl, ethyl, propyl, or any of a multitude of others; think of R as the Rest of the molecule.

prompt: "Citric acid is a tertiary alcohol." What does this statement mean?

choices.text: It has an –OH group bonded to a carbon that is itself bonded to three other carbons
It has three –OH groups
choices.why: "Tertiary" describes the carbon bearing the –OH, not the number of –OH groups.

choices.text: Its –OH group is on the third carbon of the chain
choices.why: The term counts the carbons bonded to the –OH carbon, not its position in the chain.

choices.text: Its –OH group is bonded to a carbon that also carries three hydrogens
choices.why: A carbon with an –OH and three hydrogens is bonded to no other carbon. A tertiary carbon is bonded to three carbons.

explanation: Saying citric acid is a tertiary alcohol means it has an alcohol functional group (–OH) bonded to a carbon atom that is itself bonded to three other carbons.

prompt: Which partial structure has secondary hydrogens?

choices.text: R2CH2
RCH3
choices.why: This carbon is bonded to one other carbon, so it is primary, and its hydrogens are primary.

choices.text: R3CH
choices.why: This carbon is bonded to three other carbons, so its hydrogen is tertiary.

choices.text: R4C
choices.why: This quaternary carbon has no hydrogens at all.

explanation: Primary hydrogens are attached to primary carbons (RCH3), secondary hydrogens to secondary carbons (R2CH2), and tertiary hydrogens to tertiary carbons (R3CH).

prompt: Why is there no such thing as a quaternary hydrogen?

choices.text: A quaternary carbon uses all four of its bonds on other carbons, leaving none for a hydrogen
A quaternary carbon is too crowded for hydrogens to reach, though it has an open bond
choices.why: Carbon forms four bonds. Bonded to four carbons, a quaternary carbon has no bond left over.

choices.text: Quaternary carbons do not exist in alkanes
choices.why: They do: a carbon bonded to four other carbons is quaternary, as in 2,2-dimethylpropane.

choices.text: Hydrogens are classified by their own bonds, and a hydrogen can form only one
choices.why: Hydrogens are classified by the carbon they are attached to, not by their own bonds.

explanation: Hydrogens are named after the carbon they are attached to: RCH3 (primary), R2CH2 (secondary), R3CH (tertiary). A quaternary carbon is bonded to four other carbons, so with carbon's four bonds used up it carries no hydrogen.

prompt: How many primary hydrogens does isobutane, (CH3)3CH, have?
explanation: Each of the three CH3 carbons is bonded to one other carbon, so each is primary and carries three primary hydrogens: 3 × 3 = 9. The remaining hydrogen is on the central carbon, which is bonded to three carbons, so it is tertiary.

prompt: How many secondary hydrogens does pentane, CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3, have?
explanation: The three CH2 carbons are each bonded to two other carbons, so they are secondary (R2CH2), each with two secondary hydrogens: 3 × 2 = 6. The two end CH3 carbons are primary.

prompt: How many primary carbons does 2-methylbutane, (CH3)2CHCH2CH3, have?
explanation: The three CH3 carbons are each bonded to only one other carbon, so they are primary. The CH2 carbon is bonded to two carbons (secondary), and the CH carbon to three (tertiary).
